analyses.title: Detection of imperative and declarative question–answer pairs in email conversations
analyses.research_question: Can interrogative and non-interrogative questions in email be detected and linked to their answers accurately and efficiently at sentence level by exploiting textual, contextual, and thread-structural information?
analyses.methodology: The authors used the Enron and CSpace email corpora and created human annotations for both question detection and question–answer linkage. For question detection, 350 questions were collected from randomly sampled email sentences and balanced with 350 non-questions; the questions were labeled as interrogative, imperative, declarative, or other, and three detection algorithms were compared. For question–answer pairing, four annotators labeled questions and corresponding answers in randomly selected threads, and sentence-level heuristic, classifier, and linear-regression variants were evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation repeated 50 times. Evaluation used precision, recall, and F1 under both a paragraph-oriented metric and a stricter longest-common-substring matching criterion.

key_findings.finding: Non-interrogative questions form a substantial minority of email questions: about 11% of the annotated questions were imperative, 5% declarative, and 4% other, so punctuation-only question detection misses meaningful requests.

The hand-crafted Regex detector achieved 0.959 precision, 0.860 recall, and 0.907 F1 when interrogative and non-interrogative questions were evaluated together, outperforming the tested Naive and S&M methods on F1.

The sentence-level heuristic pairing variants substantially outperformed the S&M and Naive baselines; on the union annotation set, Heuristic-LR obtained 0.5935 LCS F1 compared with 0.5108 for the strongest S&M variant and 0.1544 for Naive.

Human agreement was imperfect but reasonably strong: Fleiss kappa was 0.69 for identifying question paragraphs and 0.77 for linking answers to questions, while the two most prolific annotators reached 0.74 and 0.83 respectively.

A single answer sentence can correspond to several preceding questions; varying the maximum number of questions assigned to an answer modestly improved F1, with three questions per answer performing best on the authors' data.
Sentence-only extraction did not match annotations well when annotators selected longer answer spans, and the authors explicitly identify multi-sentence answer extraction as future work.
Restricting candidates to each person's first reply reduces the search space, but allowing later replies sometimes improves results at a substantial runtime cost.

limitations: The question-detection test set was artificially balanced at 50% questions and 50% non-questions, whereas natural email contains many more non-questions, so reported precision is not directly representative of deployment prevalence.
The exact human-created question–answer annotations used in the experiments are not reported as a released benchmark, limiting exact replication despite use of established source corpora.
The pairing model operates on individual sentences and therefore cannot adequately represent answers spanning multiple sentences or larger discourse segments.
Candidate answers are restricted to subsequent messages, to another sender, and normally to that person's first reply; this can exclude delayed or self-follow-up answers.
Detected question sentences are prohibited from serving as answers, excluding question-as-response phenomena.
The model ultimately chooses at most one answer candidate for a given question rather than representing a distributed answer across several propositions.

Although one answer may be attached to multiple questions, the study does not explicitly annotate or evaluate partial replies, which subset of a multi-question message was answered, or rates of unanswered questions.

Question-form labels and question–answer pairing annotations were produced in separate annotation exercises, preventing direct analysis of pairing behavior by interrogative versus imperative/declarative form.
raw_claims: About one fifth of the annotated email questions were not conventional interrogative sentences.
A regex system using punctuation, interrogative patterns, and hand-written non-interrogative patterns achieved above 0.9 F1 over all annotated question forms.
The pairing heuristics combine lexical similarity, thread structure, semantic information, entities, and expected answer-type features.
A candidate answer is normally restricted to a content sentence in another person's first subsequent reply to the question email.
The pairing algorithm can leave a question unmatched when no candidate exceeds its score threshold.
The implementation limits how many questions one answer can satisfy, and a limit of three worked best in the reported experiments.
Human annotators did not agree perfectly on either question boundaries or question–answer links.
The learned linear-regression heuristic produced the strongest result on the union annotation set.
Different annotators sometimes selected different answer-span lengths, exposing a mismatch with sentence-only extraction.
The experiments do not provide a direct empirical accounting of unanswered questions or explicitly labeled partial replies.

analyses.title: Annotating Abstract Pronominal Anaphora in the DAD Project
analyses.research_question: Can an extension of the MATE/GNOME annotation scheme represent abstract pronominal anaphora with non-nominal and discourse-segment antecedents in Danish and Italian in a way that annotators can apply reliably?
analyses.methodology: The DAD project extends the MATE/GNOME scheme to annotate third-person singular pronouns whose interpretation depends on verbal phrases, clauses, or discourse segments, adding antecedent syntax, semantic referent type, distance, and anaphoric-function information. The scheme was applied to heterogeneous Danish and Italian written and spoken corpora, including MapTask-style dialogues, with Danish material independently annotated by two annotators and smaller portions of the Italian material double annotated. Inter-coder agreement was evaluated with kappa for pronominal functions, antecedent identification, and semantic categories. The authors also document special handling for ambiguity and discontinuous antecedents.

key_findings.finding: The scheme explicitly represents antecedents larger than noun phrases, including verbal phrases, simple and complex clauses, and discourse segments, making proposition- and multi-proposition reference part of the annotation target.

Semantic referent labels include eventualities, fact-like entities, propositions, questions, and speech acts, allowing abstract reference to be distinguished by discourse-semantic type rather than only by span.
When more than one antecedent or referent interpretation is plausible, annotators choose a preferred interpretation but can record alternatives in a comment field.

Agreement for identifying non-NP antecedents was substantial across the evaluated subsets, with kappa values of 0.81 and 0.79 for Danish texts and dialogues and 0.89 and 0.87 for Italian texts and dialogues.
Agreement on proposition-valued referents was also high in the reported samples, with kappa values from 0.80 to 0.92 across language and modality conditions.
Discontinuous antecedents in dialogue remained difficult to encode, and the project adopted a provisional solution that links antecedent parts and then links the anaphor to the nearest part.

The authors' agreement calculation treats partially overlapping antecedent spans as full mismatches and also treats different preferred interpretations as disagreements even when both interpretations were recorded as legitimate alternatives.

limitations: Most Italian material was annotated by only one person; agreement estimates for Italian come from only three texts and two dialogues.
The authors note that expert annotators and a detailed manual may partly explain the relatively high agreement and may not predict performance by less-trained annotators.
Kappa gives no partial credit to overlapping antecedent spans, so disagreement over boundaries is conflated with completely different antecedent choices.
Although alternative interpretations can be recorded, the evaluation collapses them to a single preferred interpretation and counts different preferences as disagreement.
The treatment of discontinuous or distributed antecedents is explicitly provisional and does not provide a principled representation of multiple antecedent components.
The dialogue material is mainly MapTask-like, and the authors state that additional dialogue types remain to be annotated.
The paper focuses on anaphoric reference rather than response structure, so it does not directly annotate whether individual propositions in a multi-question turn were answered or left unanswered.
At the time of the paper an agreed-upon corpus was still being produced, and the paper does not establish availability of the exact consolidated annotations used for the reported results.
raw_claims: DAD extends an existing coreference scheme so pronouns can point to verbal phrases, clauses, and discourse segments.
The annotation distinguishes several syntactic varieties of non-nominal antecedent.
Abstract referents can be classified as eventualities, facts, propositions, questions, speech acts, or other entities.
Annotators record a preferred antecedent while retaining alternative plausible readings when ambiguity exists.
The project encountered unresolved representational difficulties with discontinuous antecedents in dialogue.
The Danish material was systematically double annotated, whereas most Italian material was not.
Reported kappa values for abstract-anaphor and non-NP-antecedent annotations were generally high.
The authors explicitly warn that kappa does not reward partially overlapping antecedent spans.
Different preferred readings are counted as disagreements even when both annotators recognize the ambiguity.
The scheme provides useful evidence that a referring expression may depend on a whole discourse segment rather than on one isolated proposition.

analyses.title: A simple but effective model for attachment in discourse parsing with multi-task learning for relation labeling
analyses.research_question: Can a relatively simple BERT-based local discourse parser jointly exploit attachment and relation-label information while supporting the multiple-parent structures required by multiparty conversation?
analyses.methodology: The authors train BERTLine on versions of the STAC multiparty game-chat corpus, encoding pairs of elementary discourse units with BERT and adding speaker-change and discourse-distance features. Attachment is treated as binary prediction over candidate parents among the preceding ten discourse units, while relation labeling uses a multi-task BERT model with separate attachment and 16-way discourse-relation heads. Predictions are evaluated with micro-averaged F1, explicitly including structures with multiple parents, and are compared with reimplemented prior discourse parsers. The authors also construct STAC-Squished by collapsing predictable adjacent game-event chains in the situated STAC data and perform ablations over structural information and multi-task learning.

key_findings.finding: The STAC discourse formalism directly permits a single discourse unit to attach to multiple earlier units, reflecting cases in which one conversational move responds to several prior moves at once.

BERTLine can predict multiple parents rather than forcing a tree, but it recovered only about 20% of the 77 multi-parent structures in the reported test set, including a small number with more than three parents.
Question–Answer-Pair is one of the 16 relation labels represented in the STAC graphs, so question/answer linkage is modeled as one discourse-relation type inside a more general attachment graph.

On standard STAC, BERTLine obtained about 73.1 attachment F1 and 56.25 relation-label F1 and was competitive with or better than the reimplemented neural alternatives, particularly for relation labeling.

Joint multi-task training of attachment and relation labeling improved relation F1 by about one point relative to the authors' pipeline formulation, supporting interdependence between deciding whether units connect and deciding how they connect.

The authors found substantial data-quality problems in standard STAC, including 488 duplicate EDUs across 60 dialogues and many Continuation relations whose interpretation becomes problematic when nonlinguistic game actions are omitted.

STAC-Squished increased the reported overall attachment and relation scores, while the authors caution that situated data can make aggregate results look better because easily predicted event-event links dominate harder linguistic attachments.

limitations: Only the preceding ten discourse units are considered as candidate parents, imposing a fixed locality bound that can exclude longer-range reply dependencies.
Although the architecture permits multiple parents, it captures only about one fifth of the annotated multi-parent structures in the reported test data.
Results aggregate relation types; the paper does not provide Question–Answer-Pair-specific precision, recall, or F1, so performance on replies to questions cannot be isolated.
STAC consists of multiparty online game chats rather than email, and the authors explicitly note uncertainty about transfer to spoken conversation and other discourse domains.
The standard STAC data contain duplicated units and discourse-label inconsistencies, while the situated version contains easy event-event chains that can inflate aggregate scores.
The newly constructed STAC-Squished corpus had not yet received the detailed error analysis and cross-corpus validation that the authors considered necessary.

The model represents attachment between discourse units but does not explicitly distinguish complete answers, partial answers, unanswered questions, or which proposition within a multi-proposition question was addressed.
raw_claims: Multiparty conversational structure is not necessarily a tree because a single turn can react to several preceding moves.
STAC represents discourse as a directed acyclic graph with labeled relations between elementary discourse units.
Question–Answer-Pair is one of the discourse relations predicted by the parser.
The attachment model independently scores several preceding units, which allows more than one parent to be selected.
Only about 20% of the test-set multi-parent structures were recovered by the reported system.
Multi-task learning couples attachment information with relation classification and modestly improves relation labeling.
Standard STAC contains duplicated dialogue material and relations affected by omitted game-state information.
Situated STAC contains numerous easily predicted adjacent event links that can distort aggregate evaluation.
STAC-Squished collapses chains of predictable nonlinguistic events and is released with the authors' implementation.
The paper does not report separate empirical results for Question–Answer-Pair links or unanswered-question behavior.

analyses.title: Identifying reference to abstract objects in dialogue
analyses.research_question: Can linguistically naive annotators reliably identify unconstrained stretches of prior dialogue that serve as antecedents for discourse-deictic references to abstract objects?
analyses.methodology: The authors conducted two annotation experiments on TRAINS-91 task-oriented planning dialogues using MMAX2. In the first experiment, 20 paid native-English-speaking undergraduates were trained to mark arbitrary text regions as segment antecedents, with 19 completing the task; in the second, four previously trained participants used a coarser scheme in which antecedents were collections of utterances, with one participant excluded and an experimenter added to the analysis. Agreement was examined using majority patterns, antecedent-boundary comparisons, and Krippendorff alpha with several set-distance measures. Custom scripts propagated discourse-region antecedents through coreference chains before analysis.

key_findings.finding: Using a criterion of at least three annotators, 35 of 181 phrase markables in the first dialogue, or 19.3%, had a plausible discourse-segment antecedent; a similar 20 of 102, or 19.6%, was obtained in the second experiment after removal of an outlying annotator.

Annotators showed meaningful but far from perfect convergence on antecedent spans: for the 16 most readily identified anaphors, Krippendorff alpha was 0.45 with Jaccard distance and 0.55 with both Dice and Passonneau distances.

Antecedent endings were more consistently localized than antecedent beginnings; among the 16 clearest cases, annotators chose the most popular beginning 42% of the time and the most popular ending 64% of the time.
Demonstrative pronouns, especially 'that', were much more readily associated with discourse-segment antecedents than personal 'it' or suggestive definite descriptions.

A simple model based on selecting an antecedent at a fixed distance from the anaphor explained much of the annotators' span behavior, suggesting that approximate antecedent vicinity may be easier to identify than exact boundaries.

Some discourse-deictic references depend on several preceding utterances and admit distinct abstract interpretations; the authors' example of 'is that correct' shows that a text-span annotation can identify the relevant prior region without distinguishing whether the referent is a plan or a fact about the plan.
The authors explicitly caution that annotation by third-party overhearers may yield lower agreement than the understanding achieved by actual dialogue participants during grounding.

limitations: Both experiments use only a very small number of dialogues from the TRAINS-91 planning domain, where references to plans are unusually frequent.
The second experiment has very few annotators; one of four participants was excluded and an experimenter was added as an annotator.
Arbitrary span boundaries are intrinsically difficult, with substantially more disagreement about where an antecedent starts than where it ends.
The text-region method cannot distinguish fine semantic alternatives such as reference to a plan versus reference to a fact about the plan.
Some agreement statistics are difficult to interpret because expected distances can become extremely large relative to local span-boundary disagreement.
A simple distance-based baseline accounts for much of human boundary placement, limiting evidence that detailed human span annotation adds substantial information beyond antecedent vicinity.
Annotators are overhearers rather than dialogue participants and lack the grounding context available to the original speakers.
The study concerns abstract reference rather than explicit question-answer alignment and therefore does not directly label partial answers or unanswered questions.
The custom Perl processing scripts and resulting experimental annotations are described but not reported as publicly released artifacts.
raw_claims: The experiments ask annotators to identify prior regions of dialogue associated with references to abstract objects.
Roughly one fifth of the evaluated markables met the authors' criterion for a plausible discourse-segment antecedent in each experiment.
Different annotators often selected overlapping rather than exactly identical antecedent spans.
Agreement was noticeably stronger for the end boundary of a discourse antecedent than for its beginning.
Demonstrative forms were much more likely than personal 'it' to receive discourse-segment antecedents.
The most consistently identified segment-anaphoric expressions in the first experiment were demonstratives referring largely to plans.
Coarser utterance-based annotation simplified the annotation task but did not remove interpretive ambiguity.
A discourse-deictic expression may package several preceding utterances into one abstract referent.
Text-span agreement alone cannot always establish which abstract semantic object the speaker intended.
A simple locality model reproduces a substantial amount of annotator behavior.

analyses.title: Resolving Discourse-Deictic Pronouns: A Two-Stage Approach to Do It
analyses.research_question: Can discourse-deictic uses of 'it', 'this', and 'that' first be identified and then resolved to verbal or clausal antecedents well enough to improve general-purpose coreference resolution?
analyses.methodology: The authors derive discourse-deictic instances from the English CoNLL-2012/OntoNotes coreference annotations and train two separate maximum-entropy components: a classifier for deciding whether a pronoun is discourse deictic and a resolver for selecting a verbal antecedent. Linguistically motivated local, syntactic, lexical-association, and selectional-preference features are used, with feature selection and pronoun-specific thresholds tuned on development data. Classification and resolution are first evaluated separately using precision, recall, and F1, including an oracle-classification condition, and then stacked on the Berkeley and HOTCoref NP-coreference systems. The authors additionally manually analyze 50 development-set decisions to diagnose system and annotation errors.

key_findings.finding: The test data contain 252 discourse-deictic instances among 2,075 occurrences of 'it', 'that', and 'this', with large differences in prevalence by pronoun and especially strong class imbalance for 'it'.

The discourse-deixis classifier achieved 35.2 precision, 42.9 recall, and 38.6 F1 overall, versus 34.8 F1 for the stronger naive classification baseline, although performance remained low because of class imbalance and limited discourse-level features.
With gold discourse-deixis classification, the resolver achieved 48.2 overall F1, compared with 39.3 for the nearest-verb baseline and 41.0 for the Müller-style model.

Using predicted rather than oracle classifications greatly reduced resolution performance to 22.2 overall F1, but the two-stage resolver still outperformed both comparison resolvers under the same condition.

Adding the two-stage predictions to Berkeley and HOTCoref produced small increases in their overall CoNLL scores, from 61.71 to 61.73 and from 61.64 to 61.69 respectively; most tested differences were statistically significant, though the attainable improvement with oracle discourse-deixis information was much larger.

Manual error analysis exposed substantial gold-standard problems: among categorized non-matching cases, 11.4% were attributed to missing annotations, 20% to multiple acceptable antecedents, and another 20% to cases where system and gold decisions were both debatable.

The authors found cases where a pronoun packages a fragment or set of preceding clauses and where more than one elaborating clause is an acceptable antecedent, directly challenging annotation guidelines and metrics that require one unique verbal antecedent.

Because multiple, overlapping, or debatable antecedents are frequent enough to affect evaluation, the authors argue for a more flexible evaluation measure rather than exact agreement with one gold antecedent.

limitations: Classification performance is low, especially for discourse-deictic 'it', whose positive examples are highly imbalanced.
Most features use relatively local context and the authors acknowledge that important discourse-level cues are not modeled.
The CoNLL/OntoNotes annotations were not designed specifically for discourse deixis and contain missing, partial, ambiguous, and sometimes questionable antecedent annotations.
The evaluation assumes one exact antecedent even though the error analysis finds multiple acceptable or overlapping antecedents and pronouns that package sets of clauses.
The manual error analysis covers only 50 system decisions on the development set.
The exact subset of resolution features selected for one reported model is omitted for brevity, reducing exact reproducibility from the paper alone.
The system is limited to English and to the pronouns 'it', 'this', and 'that'.
The task concerns discourse deixis rather than reply-to-question alignment, so it does not directly identify which questions or propositions in a multi-question turn receive answers.
No implementation release is identified in the paper.
raw_claims: The system separates discourse-deixis recognition from antecedent resolution instead of solving both in one decision.
The CoNLL-2012 test set supplies hundreds of discourse-deictic examples for 'it', 'this', and 'that', but their class distributions differ sharply.
The learned classifier only modestly improves over a simple pronoun-specific classification baseline.
Resolution is substantially easier when the system is told which pronouns are discourse deictic.
Classification errors therefore impose a major bottleneck on end-to-end antecedent resolution.
Adding discourse-deictic links gives small but measurable improvements to two general coreference systems.
Manual inspection shows that some apparent model errors are actually absent or incomplete gold annotations.
Several inspected cases permit more than one reasonable clausal antecedent.
Some pronouns summarize or package a sequence of related clauses rather than referring cleanly to one proposition.
A strict single-antecedent scorer can penalize linguistically reasonable system predictions.
The authors conclude that discourse-deixis corpora and evaluation methods need to represent ambiguity more faithfully.
